tldr: In long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks where a humanoid cleans up multiple objects in sequence, this study achieves advanced task planning via imagined rollouts by combining frozen low-level motor skills with a macro world model that predicts state transitions at the skill level.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed LUCID method. On the left, a low-level controller (LLC) with diverse whole-body motion skills is trained using adversarial imitation learning and then frozen. On the right, a macro world model (WM) predicting environment transitions at the skill level and a high-level controller (HLC) that makes long-term decisions through imagination are jointly trained.
overview:
Having a humanoid robot navigate through rooms and tidy up multiple pieces of furniture and daily items is one of the ultimate goals in robotics. However, even if individual motions like walking and grasping objects are mastered, chaining them smoothly over extended periods without failures has been extremely difficult. Most existing works rely on finite-state machines (FSMs) to switch actions or conveniently reset the robot's pose between subtasks. As a result, they lack autonomous planning that accounts for how earlier actions impact subsequent work environments.

To address this, the authors developed a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework called "LUCID." The core idea is "temporal abstraction." Instead of predicting joint angles at every single step, they let a low-level controller execute meaningful skills, while a world model predicts only the "macro-dynamics"—how objects and the robot change after running that skill for a few seconds. Then, by performing "imagined rollouts" inside this model, the high-level policy optimizes action decisions that look ahead to future subtasks.

Evaluated on multi-object rearrangement tasks in a physics simulator, LUCID significantly outperformed existing baseline methods in task completion rates. It maintained stable performance across unseen room layouts and even on longer tasks involving cleaning up 5 objects (longer than seen during training), demonstrating that a macro predictive model is remarkably effective for long-horizon humanoid whole-body coordination.
contributions: Built a macro-dynamics world model that predicts task progress at the skill level (macro timescale) rather than the joint level, enabling high-level planning through imagined rollouts.
Designed and froze a reusable, structured latent skill space (LLC) using adversarial imitation learning and an interaction curriculum, allowing intuitive commands from the high level.
Achieved a full-task success rate more than 30 points higher than baseline methods in multi-object sequential rearrangement tasks across rooms, without inserting artificial pose resets midway.

sections.heading: Why is long-horizon whole-body manipulation so hard for humanoids?
sections.summary: Sequential multi-object rearrangement by humanoids requires both versatile whole-body motor skills and long-term decision making. However, existing hierarchical methods and finite-state machines cannot foresee the impact of current actions on subsequent subtasks, leading to breakdown over long executions. To resolve this, this work introduces a world model predicting transitions at the skill level and proposes "LUCID" to optimize action plans in imagination.
sections.details:
For individual skills like locomotion or lifting objects, humanoid robots can now move very naturally and smoothly thanks to physics simulations and imitation learning. However, when it comes to long-horizon sequential tasks such as tidying up multiple objects to designated target spots in order, the difficulty skyrockets.

Prevailing approaches have relied on task-specific controllers or handcrafted rules and finite-state machines (FSMs) to switch between locomotion and manipulation phases. However, these methods cannot account for the downstream impact of intermediate decisions, such as where placing one object might later obstruct picking up the next.

While "world models" that predict environmental transitions have garnered attention, attempting to predict fine joint-level physics simulations over long horizons using neural networks for high-DoF, contact-rich humanoids causes errors to accumulate rapidly and diverge.

Addressing this issue, this paper argues that "temporal abstraction" is key. Instead of predicting fine joint trajectories every millisecond, it learns a world model that predicts only macro-level changes: "how the object and robot move after executing a given skill for several steps." This inspired the LUCID framework, seamlessly bridging low-level motor control with long-term predictive reasoning.

sections.heading: Trends in physics-based motion generation and robot world models
sections.summary: This work lies at the intersection of three fields: physics-based motion generation via adversarial imitation learning, hierarchical reinforcement learning separating high and low levels, and world models predicting environmental dynamics. While prior studies focused on joint-level control or single-task optimization, LUCID stands out by running a macro world model over a frozen, structured skill space.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main research threads.

The first is "physics-based motion generation." Adversarial imitation learning methods, such as AMP (Adversarial Motion Priors) and ASE (Adversarial Skill Embeddings), have successfully acquired natural and reusable motion primitives from large mocap datasets. Recently, this has been extended to whole-body furniture manipulation, yet autonomously switching these skills across long-horizon scenarios has remained an open challenge.

The second is "hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL)." Decoupling low-level motor skills from a high-level scheduler is a well-established design that has shown success in quadrupedal robots. However, training the high level with model-free reinforcement learning demands massive trial-and-error interactions and struggles with forward-looking action selection.

The third is "world models in robotics." Methods like DreamerV3 and DayDreamer have shown strong results by having robots predict environmental changes from their actions with neural networks and training policies entirely inside their imagination. Nonetheless, conventional world models primarily model joint torques or continuous low-level actions directly, suffering from compounding predictive errors over long horizons. Building on these foundations, LUCID freezes the low-level controller in advance and trains the world model exclusively on state transitions driven by macro skill commands.

sections.heading: The LUCID architecture: Structured skill learning and a macro world model
sections.summary: LUCID is trained in two stages. In the first stage, a low-level controller (LLC) featuring a semantically structured latent skill space is trained via adversarial imitation and a three-stage curriculum, then frozen. In the second stage, a world model (WM) predicting macro environmental changes under the LLC, along with a high-level controller (HLC) aiming to achieve goals through imagined trial-and-error, are trained jointly.
sections.details:
The overall LUCID system consists of two main components: the low-level controller (LLC) and the macro-dynamics world model (WM) combined with the high-level controller (HLC).

### Learning the Structured Latent Skill Space (LLC)
The LLC receives the current robot and object observations $s_t^L$ along with a latent variable $z_t$ provided by the high level, and outputs PD control joint targets $a_t$. Rather than scattering skills arbitrarily across a spherical surface like ASE, this method introduces a "structured latent space" where one-hot anchor vectors are assigned to meaningful skills (approach, carry, release, etc.), with fine variations represented in the surrounding continuous space. The training combines an adversarial imitation discriminator reward $r_t^D$ and a task reward $r_t^G$, accompanied by a three-stage curriculum ("grasp and lift", "carry and place", "step back and transition to next task") to reliably build skills that follow instructions before freezing the parameters completely.

### Macro-Dynamics World Model (WM)
When the frozen LLC receives the latent variable $z_t$ and guidance offset $p_t^g$ chosen by the high level, it runs autonomously in the simulator for $K=20$ steps (approx. 0.67 seconds). These $K$ steps are treated as a single "macro-transition." The WM predicts continuous changes in robot and object positions and lift heights (residuals $f_\theta$), discrete flags indicating whether the object was placed at the goal ($g_\theta$), and a continuation probability $\hat{\zeta}_t$ indicating whether the task terminated in failure. It is trained using mean squared error for continuous values and binary cross-entropy loss for flags.

### High-Level Learning via Imagined Rollouts (HLC)
The HLC actor $\pi_{H,\varphi}$ and critic $V_\xi$ are trained using an approach similar to DreamerV3. Actual states are sampled from a replay buffer, and the newly updated WM "imagines" future rollouts up to $Q=12$ steps ahead. Because it involves discrete skill selection, the actor update employs score function estimation (REINFORCE-style), while the critic uses distributional value learning. To stabilize early exploration, it is warm-started with behavioral cloning (BC) from a geometric oracle, with its weight gradually decayed to zero to transition toward an autonomous policy.

captions.F1: Overview of the LUCID architecture. In the LLC training phase (left), the skill space is organized using an oracle and a discriminator, then frozen. In the subsequent HLC training phase (right), the WM is updated using macro-transition buffers collected from the simulator, and the HLC's long-horizon policy is optimized through imagined rollouts inside the WM.

sections.heading: Validation in complex rooms: Overwhelming robustness in sequential rearrangement
sections.summary: LUCID was evaluated on a multi-object rearrangement benchmark using Isaac Gym. Compared to baselines, full-task success rates improved by more than 30 points in both familiar and unseen room layouts. Furthermore, it maintained high success rates even in long tasks involving up to 5 objects (exceeding training settings), with ablation studies confirming the importance of both the world model and the structured latent space.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Experiments were conducted in Isaac Gym with a humanoid model featuring 15 links and 28 joints. The task was to sequentially pick up objects scattered on the floor and place them at goal locations across four room layouts: living room, bedroom, kitchen, and warehouse. Tasks included 62 in-distribution (ID) setups matching the training layouts and 20 out-of-distribution (OOD) setups with unseen arrangements.

Baselines included motion-tracking-based "InterMimic", finite-state-machine skill-switching "TokenHSI", and "HumanVLA" which calls single-object manipulation policies sequentially. Because the baselines cannot transition autonomously between subtasks, they were granted an advantageous setup where the robot was teleported near the next object as soon as it placed an object.

### Quantitative Evaluation and Robustness in Long-Horizon Tasks
In tasks requiring sequential placement of two objects, LUCID operated fully autonomously without resetting the robot, achieving a second subtask success rate (SR2) of 73.4% in ID (best baseline HumanVLA: 39.8%) and 68.4% in OOD (baseline: 37.0%). A notable trait is that the drop in success rate from the first object to the second was remarkably small.

Furthermore, in scaled-up long-horizon tasks cleaning up to 5 objects (Figure F3), baselines completely collapsed by the 4th and 5th objects (success rates of 0–5%) due to compounding errors, whereas LUCID retained a success rate of about 56% on the 3rd object and 21% even on the 5th object.

### Ablation Studies: What Drove the Success?
Comparing LUCID against model-free (MF) reinforcement learning, imagined rollouts using the WM improved SR2 by 14.2 points in ID and 20.3 points in OOD (Table 2). This demonstrates that lookahead via the WM is effective even under sparse rewards.

Additionally, in an ablation comparing the presence versus absence of structure in the latent space (Figure F6), an unstructured space (ASE-style spherical sampling) retained motion diversity but failed to develop reliable object-lifting skills, resulting in a 0% task success rate. This indicates that a structured interface with explicit anchors aligned to the task is indispensable.

captions.F2: Execution snapshots of LUCID across various room environments. The high-level controller chooses appropriate skills based on the situation—blue (locomotion), green (carry), red (release), yellow (approach), and purple (transition to next)—completing sequential operations without resetting the robot once.
captions.F3: Success rate curves as the number of objects to rearrange increases. While baselines drop to near-zero success by the 4th and 5th objects, LUCID (purple line) persistently maintains success across long task chains of up to 5 objects.
captions.F5: Comparison between the world model's multi-step predictions up to 12 steps ahead (orange dashed line) and simulator ground truth (black solid line). The model captures dynamics directly tied to task progress, such as object-to-goal distances and lift heights, with high accuracy.
captions.F6: Comparison between structured and unstructured latent skill spaces. As the bottom-right plot demonstrates, the unstructured interface completely fails to produce motions that lift objects to the required height, highlighting the critical importance of structuring the space.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: LUCID substantially advances long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation by uniting frozen structured motor skills with imagined planning via a skill-level macro world model. Current limitations include reliance on privileged simulator state information, leaving vision-based visual control and real-robot humanoid deployments as promising directions for future work.
sections.details:
This paper presented LUCID, a new hierarchical framework enabling humanoid robots to autonomously tidy up multiple scattered objects. Its core essence lies in adopting "appropriate temporal abstraction" for both motion generation and environment prediction. By equipping the low-level controller with a task-aligned skill space and predicting/optimizing only the macro outcomes of those skills at the high level, the framework avoids error explosions that plague joint-level physics simulation forecasts.

On the other hand, as acknowledged by the authors, the current system has clear limitations. Primarily, it directly receives privileged state observations from the simulator, such as exact 3D positions and velocities of the robot and objects. Operating in the real world will require estimating states from sensors like RGB-D cameras or extending the framework to a vision-based world model. Moreover, evaluated tasks, object shapes, and robot morphologies remain limited. Going forward, handling visual inputs and achieving Sim-to-Real transfer across diverse objects and physical robot hardware represent crucial research directions.

takeaways: In long-horizon humanoid manipulation, a macro world model that predicts task state transitions at the skill level, rather than joint-level physics, is an extremely effective way to prevent compounding errors.

Simply embedding diverse motions into a low-level skill space is not enough; anchoring the space with structured targets aligned to task phases (approach, grasp, carry, retreat) makes the difference between success and failure.

Once skills are frozen, a high-level planner can alternate between the simulator's true environment and imagined rollouts in the world model to learn robust sequential planning with high sample efficiency.
limitations: Relies on privileged geometric simulator information, such as robot joint states and exact 3D object coordinates, without supporting end-to-end control directly from camera images.
Evaluations remain confined to specific rigid objects and room layouts within Isaac Gym; generalization to deformable objects or dynamic obstacles is untested.
Sim-to-Real transfer to physical humanoid hardware has not yet been demonstrated, leaving robustness against real-world gaps (contact dynamics, sensor noise) unknown.
